title: Subject-Verb Agreement

sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Agreement is a matching rule with two settings: how many, and which person. If the subject is one third-person thing, the present-tense verb takes the -s form ("the nurse checks"); if the subject is more than one, the verb drops it ("the nurses check"). Two things the verb does not care about: gender, and distance. A long phrase can sit between the subject and the verb, and the match still has to hold across it.

### Question 2

Test each sentence by swapping the subject for "it" or "they." One blood pressure is an "it," and you would say "it remains," so "remains" is right. Signs, students, and charts are all "they," and "they" takes were, study, and need. One warning about the -s ending: on a noun it usually means plural, but on a present-tense verb it means singular. That reversal is what makes "the charts needs" sound acceptable to the ear when it is not.

### Question 3

Words like everyone and each sound like they cover a crowd, but grammatically they pick people out one at a time, which is exactly what "each" means. So the verb stays in the form you would use after "he" or "she": "Everyone needs a wristband." When a phrase like "of the residents" follows, cover it with your finger and read what is left: "Each ... receives." The plural noun in that phrase is bait.

### Question 4

Cover the words "of sterile gloves" with your thumb and read what is left: "The box ___ on the shelf." One box, so "is." The gloves are just description riding along, like a label on the outside of the box, and a label does not get to choose the verb. The trick works because your ear matches the verb to whatever it heard last, and covering the phrase takes that last word away.

### Question 5

"And" works like a plus sign: one thing plus another gives more than one, so the verb goes plural. "Or" works like a choose-one sign: only one of the two will actually do the action, so the verb looks at whichever partner is standing next to it and copies that one. Because the verb depends on order with "or," reversing the two nouns can change the correct verb, and writers often park the plural one last so the sentence reads smoothly.

### Question 6

A collective noun is a container word: it names many people but points at one container. If the container moves as a whole, use the singular verb: the team meets, the staff decides. If you really need to show the people inside acting separately, do not fight the container word by bolting on a plural verb; open the container and name the people, as in "the team members meet." Rewriting the subject is quieter than a verb your reader will flag as an error.

### Question 7

"There" is a placeholder that saves a seat at the table; it is not the guest. The actual guest arrives after the verb. So before choosing is or are, read past the placeholder and count what shows up: one form arriving means "there is," three forms arriving means "there are." If the sentence still feels slippery, rewrite it without the placeholder at all: "Three consent forms sit on the desk" puts the subject back in front where the verb can see it.

### Question 8

Ask yourself: sixty percent of what? If the answer is countable items, such as containers, the verb goes plural—"are full." If the answer is a single mass, such as the supply or the medication, the verb goes singular—"is gone." The percentage by itself tells you nothing about number; it is a share of something else, and that something else after "of" is the real subject matter. Note how this reverses the usual advice to ignore the "of" phrase, so it is worth memorizing as its own case.

### Question 9

With neither...nor, treat the verb as nearsighted: it can only make out the subject standing right beside it. Here that neighbor is "two technicians," so the verb becomes "were." Swap the two elements and the correct verb changes with them, which is a good self-check: if flipping the order flips the verb, you are applying the rule correctly. When the result sounds awkward either way, rewrite as two clauses: "The charge nurse was not available, and neither were the technicians."

### Question 10

Ask who is actually working nights. In "one of the nurses who work nights," a whole group works nights and Maria is one of them, so the verb matches the group: work. Add "the only," and the group of night workers shrinks to Maria alone, so it becomes works. A quick test: move the clause to the front. "Of the nurses who work nights, Maria is one" sounds right, and it exposes which noun the who is pointing back to.

### Question 11

"The number" names one specific figure, like the single total written at the bottom of a chart, so the verb is singular: has declined. "A number of" is not really about a figure at all; it is a roundabout way of saying "several," so the things after it are the real actors and the verb goes plural. Test it by substituting the word several: if "several readmissions were preventable" still says what you mean, use the plural verb.

### Question 12

A linking verb looks like an equals sign, but grammar does not treat the two sides as interchangeable: the verb takes its number from the subject on the left, never from the complement on the right. One cause on the left means "is," no matter how many items are listed after it. If "is" followed by a long list grates on your ear, that is a signal to flip the sentence so the list becomes the subject, and then "are" is genuinely correct.
